title: Design a class that is initialized with a value K and an initial list of numbers, and supports an add operation that inserts a new number and returns the Kth largest element among all numbers seen so far.
shortTitle: Kth Largest in a Stream — maintain a min-heap of size K
topicTitle: Design a class that is initialized with a value K and an initial list of numbers

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Largest in a Stream keeps a min-heap of size K holding the K largest values seen so far. On add, push the new value and, if the heap exceeds K, remove the smallest; the heap root is then always the Kth largest. Each add costs log K and the query is the root in constant time.

When a new donation comes, you add it to the shortlist and, if the list grew to six, you drop the smallest. The smallest on that shortlist of five is always the fifth-largest overall.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Largest in a Stream keeps a min-heap of size K holding the K largest values seen so far. On add, push the new value and, if the heap exceeds K, remove the smallest; the heap root is then always the Kth largest. Each add costs log K and the query is the root in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine always knowing the fifth-largest donation received so far as donations keep arriving. You keep a shortlist of exactly the five biggest. When a new donation comes, you add it to the shortlist and, if the list grew to six, you drop the smallest. The smallest on that shortlist of five is always the fifth-largest overall.

**One line to remember:** A size-K min-heap holds the K largest so far; each add pushes then trims to K, and the root is the Kth largest.

sections.s2_technical:
The constructor builds a min-heap and feeds the initial numbers through the same add logic so the heap ends holding at most the K largest. For example: `for (int n : nums) add(n);`.

The add operation pushes the new value, then if the heap size exceeds K it removes the smallest element, keeping exactly the K largest values. For example: `heap.offer(val); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();`. After this the root is the smallest of the K largest, which is the Kth largest overall.

Returning the answer is simply reading the heap root, a constant-time peek. For example: `return heap.peek();`. The heap never holds more than K elements, so memory is bounded by K regardless of how many values stream in.

Each add is a single push and possibly a single poll, each log K, so the per-add cost is log K, far cheaper than re-sorting. A senior nuance is that when fewer than K values have been seen, the heap simply holds all of them and its root is still the correct answer for the current count, and that this structure is the canonical way to answer a repeated Kth-largest query on a growing stream without unbounded memory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a fraud dashboard continuously displays the Kth largest transaction amount as new transactions stream in, used as a live high-value watermark. The system must add amounts and return the current Kth largest on each add. This is exactly how Kth Largest in a Stream works.

Problem 2 — The stream is unbounded, so the structure must hold only K values, not the whole history. This is exactly why the size-K min-heap is used, bounding memory at K.

The mini-project builds a `KthLargestStream` initialized with K and seed amounts, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that adds amounts and prints the Kth largest after each.

sections.s5_journey:
The input seeds K equal to three with amounts 4000, 5000, 8000, 2000, then adds 3000, 10000, 1000.

Step 1: Seeding pushes 4000, 5000, 8000, then pushes 2000 making size four and drops the smallest 2000, leaving 4000, 5000, 8000. The root is 4000, the third largest.

Step 2: Add 3000. Pushed, size four, drops the smallest 3000, so the heap stays 4000, 5000, 8000. The root is still 4000.

Step 3: Add 10000. Pushed, size four, drops the smallest 4000, leaving 5000, 8000, 10000. The root is 5000, the new third largest.

Step 4: Add 1000. Pushed, size four, drops the smallest 1000 immediately, so the heap stays 5000, 8000, 10000. The root is 5000.

Step 5: At every step the heap held at most three values, so memory never grew with the stream length.

Step 6: The returned Kth largest tracked the live high-value watermark: 4000, then 4000, then 5000, then 5000.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  K=3, size-K min-heap holds the 3 largest so far:

  seed 4000,5000,8000,2000 → {4000,5000,8000} root=4000
  add 3000  → drop 3000  → {4000,5000,8000} root=4000
  add 10000 → drop 4000  → {5000,8000,10000} root=5000 ★
  add 1000  → drop 1000  → {5000,8000,10000} root=5000

  root = Kth largest, always; heap size capped at K.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Largest in a Stream asks me to return the Kth largest value among everything seen so far, repeatedly, as new values arrive. The clean solution is a min-heap capped at size K that always holds exactly the K largest values seen. Its root, the smallest of those K, is by definition the Kth largest overall.

The add operation pushes the new value and, if the heap then exceeds K, removes the smallest, trimming back to the K largest. After that, I read the root in constant time to answer the query. The constructor simply feeds the initial numbers through the same add logic, so the heap settles into holding the K largest from the start, and when fewer than K values have been seen the heap holds all of them and the root is still the correct current answer.

The property interviewers want me to articulate is that the heap never grows beyond K, so memory is bounded no matter how long the stream runs, and each add is just one push and at most one poll at log K cost. This is the canonical way to answer a repeated Kth-largest query on an unbounded stream without storing the whole history.

In my project at National Bank of India, a fraud dashboard showed the Kth largest transaction amount as a live high-value watermark that updated with every incoming transaction. The size-K min-heap let the dashboard respond to each new amount in logarithmic time while holding only K values, so the watermark stayed current without the memory growing as the day's transaction stream lengthened.
